summary:
A syndicated Fortune piece (via Allwork.Space) reports that after a weak start to 2026, U.S. hiring intentions are rebounding. Robert Half data shows 66% of U.S. employers plan to increase permanent hiring in the second half of 2026, up from 60% in H1 and 57% a year earlier. Additionally 56% say they will add contract talent to access specialized skills, and nearly half have canceled projects because of skills gaps. Michelle Reisdorf of Robert Half says employers have hit a boiling point where waiting to hire is no longer an option, and that they are investing in talent tied to business priorities rather than adding headcount for its own sake.

Demand by function: technology (78%), healthcare (75%), finance and accounting (74%), marketing and creative (65%), legal (58%), human resources (56%), and administration and customer support (52%). Despite AI-driven cuts to support roles, HR and admin/customer support remain in demand. Hardest skills to find are industry-specific knowledge (47%), software proficiency (42%), and leadership (40%).

The labor market backdrop remains grim. June added only 57,000 roles, under half the prior month. Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported 1.2 million announced job cuts last year, up 58% from roughly 760,000 in 2024, the highest level since 2020 and comparable to 2008's 1.22 million. New York Fed data shows the average perceived probability of finding a job after job loss fell to 43.1% in December 2025, down 4.2% year over year and a record low since tracking began in 2013. Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao says lower-income and non-degree workers feel the market is not working for them. WSJ analysis found workers aged 25 to 34 averaged 19 weeks unemployed versus 26 weeks for those 55 to 64; 24% of laid-off Gen X and boomer workers never found a new job, and 11% took a pay cut.
